newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Internet guru sees Asian restrictions failing.
newsitem.headline: Internet guru sees Asian restrictions failing.

text.p: Efforts by Asian nations to restrict access to the Internet and censor its contents can be sidestepped easily and are likely to fail, a world authority on Internet security said Wednesday.
"I think they (restrictions) are of limited effectiveness," Bill Cheswick of Bell Laboratories said in an interview.
Cheswick also said the rise of intranets -- internal corporate networks that mimic the Internet -- have made it easier for hackers to attack corporate computers.
His comments follow a resolution by Southeast Asian broadcasters and officials at an ASEAN forum meeting this month to police the Internet and block access to sites that run counter to Asian values.
The resolution comes as Singapore and Chinese authorities tighten limits on Internet access, citing concerns about offensive material.
The restrictions, which prevent access to some sites on the vast, worldwide computer network, can go some way to curbing free speech, but computer hackers can evade them, said Cheswick.

"You can sneak these things in," he said, explaining that a hacker could break into a government computer system, hide banned material there using encryption techniques and alert other Internet users on how to access it.

"You've got encryption, you've got steganography (messages hidden in innocuous text). I can encode this data, so ... I can get it through," he said after addressing an Asia-Pacific Internet conference in Melbourne.
Asian leaders are mainly concerned about pornography in cyberspace as well as information that could spark religious and racial tensions and the activist activities of exiled dissidents.

Singapore, seen at the forefront of Internet regulation within the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), forces its Internet service providers to use computer "proxy servers" which block requests for undesirable material.
ASEAN is comprised by Singapore, Brunei, Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam. Australia has also expressed concern about the use of the Internet for pedophile rings.
Britain's Financial Times last week reported that dozens of World Wide Web sites had been closed to Chinese Internet users in an effort by Beijing to muzzle publication of anti-Communist party views.

Cheswick pointed Wednesday to a recent U.S. example where hackers, aggrieved by government calls to regulate the Internet, tampered with the Web page of the U.S. Justice Department, swapping a swastika for the department's logo.
Hacking via the Internet, which boasts over 35 million users, is on the increase worldwide with commercial targets becoming prone to larger attacks, Cheswick said.
"There are more people (using computers), they're learning more ... the hackers are out there training and there are also bigger and bigger commercial attempts to hack," he said.

The advent of large corporate networks, or "intranets," and the growing use of user-friendly internal Web pages as stores of corporate data, also are making firms more vulnerable to hacker infiltration, he said.

"Before that was around, if I had broken into your corporate network, how do I find the payroll, or whatever? If it's easier for people inside the company to find, it's easier for spies to find it as well," Cheswick said.
